entries.title: Large tasks: Discussion, a pre-planner, and the pieces as darn runs inside the task's beam
entries.brief: Discussion decides scope, a pre-planner splits it into contracted pieces, each piece runs as darn from the task's beam, a whole-task perch reviews, then align and land
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-22)

A large task runs as a loom whose implementation is a set of darn runs inside its own beam:

1. Task A runs Discussion as today; Discussion stays the one agent that talks with the operator and decides scope.
2. A pre-planner breaks the decided scope into smaller pieces that together make up the whole scope.
   Each piece gets a contract: what it takes in, the behaviour it delivers, the names it exports to other pieces, and which pieces it depends on; not the inside, which the darn finds itself.
3. Each piece becomes a darn task with that contract and its part of the decision record and `relevant.md`, with `depends_on` between pieces.
4. The next producer turns Task A's worktree into a beam.
5. The darn tasks run from beam A as ordinary darn runs and merge back into Task A's branch, not `main`; pieces with no dependency between them run in parallel.
6. When every darn has merged back, a Task A-wide perch reviews the whole and makes small fixes.
7. The rest is as today: Parent-Align, PR, landing, so `main` takes Task A whole.

## Why

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: a loom run carries a fixed cost of about $23, mostly Plan and the review rounds, and the Plan writer reads about 250k of context before it writes (91% of its peak).
Darn's fixed cost is about $2.60.
Split this way, each darn reads only its piece once, plans and implements it, and is reviewed by its own perch; Discussion and the whole-task perch keep loom's scope and overall check.
It came out of discussing sub-planners for the Plan writer (note `plan-writer-context`): pieces small enough to plan and implement together are darn runs.

## Depends on

The beam setup: `orch-any-worktree` is landed (dd11ab09f: beams, pairs from a parent pair, `lym beam create`, `land`; its `promote` was removed by `beam-start-and-ownership`, which also added `lym beam start` and the `pawl` recipe), and `umbrella-daemon` is landed too (c2a03a885: dobby, a per-beam daemon that drives runs).
Earlier wording: `orch-any-worktree` (umbrella tasks spawning and landing from their own worktree) and `umbrella-daemon` (a daemon per beam that drives its runs).

## Open

- Contract precision: too loose and pieces collide, too tight and the pre-planner becomes today's Plan writer.
- A darn that finds its contract wrong stops and escalates to Task A instead of improvising; dependent pieces wait.
- What drives the darns inside the beam: dobby now starts and drives a beam's ready tasks (c2a03a885); open is how Task A's run waits for them.
- How large the whole-task perch's fixes may be before they mean a piece failed.
- Quality against full loom: each piece gets one perch instead of Plan and Webster review; measure follow-up fixes against loom runs.
- Cost: Discussion, pre-planner, N darns and the whole-task perch against a loom run of the same size.

## Review placement (operator, 2026-10-22)

- The pre-plan gets a perch, but the pre-plan is far smaller than today's plan format: pieces and their contracts, not cards.
- No perch per darn: a review per batch proved far too expensive in Millhouse, and a perch per piece is the same.
  The pieces run as darn with review off (`code_max_bounces: 0`, since `code-review-one-perch` made darn's perch the Code-Review perch), each still passing its own gate and tests; the whole-task perch after the last merge-back is the code review, as Webster's round over the whole diff is today.
  For scale, a darn perch costs about $1.30 per run in the audit window.
- The pieces run tests as they go, the way Webster's card gate runs after every card.

## Piece recipe `stitch` (operator, 2026-10-22)

The pieces run on their own recipe, `stitch`, derived from darn, not on a darn profile: rows go away, not only bounds.
Alignment per piece is pointless when the piece is a closed, synchronised share of an umbrella that is aligned whole.

- Kept: Preflight; the writer, on Sonnet, briefed by its pre-plan contract.
- Dropped: Code-Bouncer and the Code-Burler review/fix rows (review off), Describe and PR-Review.
  Since `loom-tail-review` (2026-10-24) darn has no Merge-In, Publish, PR-Align or PR-Gate rows; its Finalize merges the parent in under the lock.
- Finalize merges into the umbrella branch under the parent lock instead of landing on `main`.
- Friction-Reflect runs once per umbrella, not per piece.
- A `stitch` task runs only inside an umbrella; it cannot run alone.
- Estimate (orch, not measured): about $2-2.50 per piece against about $6 for a darn with review.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24): once `stitch` exists, Codex could run the pre-planner, as a role apart from the Claude-written code (see note `codex-engine`).

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23): darn itself as the piece implementer

Once `loom-tail-review` has landed, darn itself may serve as the pieces' implementer, since that task removes much of the run tail's ceremony, such as the pull request.
Whether `stitch` then stays a recipe of its own, or becomes darn with the tail rows a piece does not need turned off, is to be weighed against what `loom-tail-review` lands.

## Test depth of a piece (operator, 2026-10-23)

A piece run does not run the full suite a standalone darn runs before it lands.
The umbrella runs the full suite once, after every piece has merged back.
Which tiers a piece's own gates run is open; the gate key per recipe row is stated in `internal/gateslot`'s doc (`gate-runs-once`, landed): a piece's rows read `darn-write`, `code-burler-fix` and `finalize`.

## Pre-plan depth (orch, 2026-10-24, not decided)

- A coarse pre-plan leaves design to the pieces, so each piece needs an Opus writer.
- A detailed pre-plan carries the design, so Sonnet pieces may do, at the cost of a heavier pre-planner.
- Pieces cannot be counted on to run in parallel: `tools/plandag/plandag.sh` on `loom-tail-review`'s plan found 52 cards, a critical path of 20 and a mean parallelism of 2.6.
  A beam's gain is then mostly smaller review scopes, not wall time.

entries.title: A task that turns out to be a project is refiled as a project, keeping its Discussion findings
entries.brief: The agent files a note with its findings and tells the orch; the operator decides, then the run ends and a new beam spawns from the parent
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-25, operator 2026-10-30)

A beam is made from a project entry with `lym beam create`, and its life is one batten run over that entry with the `pawl` recipe.
`lym beam promote` is removed: switching a running task's worktree into a beam halfway proved messy.
A task can still turn out too large while its Discussion runs, and then it has to become a project instead.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-30)

The agent that finds this out, in Discussion or in a research or darn run, files a note on the board with everything it found, tells its parent, the orch, and ends its turn.
It never files a project or a task, and starts nothing: only the operator decides what becomes a task or a project.
The orch puts the finding to the operator; when the operator decides on a project, the old run ends and the project is created and spawned as a new beam from the parent, never from the old task's worktree.
Nothing is switched in place.

The note must keep what the agent learned: its body holds the Discussion writer's findings and decisions, so they become the beam's starting design and are not left behind in the old run's records history.
Note `loom-beam-darns` is a related shape, where a large loom task turns into a beam and runs its pieces as darn runs inside it.

## Open design points

- How the agent tells its parent: a message to the orch with the note's slug, and whether the run stops by itself afterwards or waits for the orch to end it.
- How the run ends once the operator has decided: the orch ends it with `lym batten cancel <slug> --remove`.
- How the note becomes the project entry and its beam: the orch turns it into a project entry after the operator's go-ahead and runs `lym beam create`, with the old task's entry removed or marked superseded in the same step.
- Whether the old run's code commits, if any, are kept or dropped.
- With dobby as the only driver of a beam's runs (only beams have a dobby, and the prime is the root beam), a worktree that is to have worktrees under it must be a beam from the start, so this route is the only way a task's scope grows into a tree of runs.

entries.title: Ideas from r/ClaudeCode "one line in your CLAUDE.md": fit for LoomYard and bench measures
entries.brief: About 30 ideas judged against our stencils and rules; top 8 ranked for a bench, a few cheap enough without one
entries.body:
# r/ClaudeCode "What's the one line in your CLAUDE.md that made the biggest difference?" — review for LoomYard

Status (2026-10-30): the repository's `CLAUDE.md` is deleted (`claude-md-lym-rules-out`), so each `CLAUDE.md:N` citation below names a line that no longer exists; its rule now lives in PATTERN, the stencils or `lym orch rules`.
Status: the operator decides whether a research task with a bench is drafted from section 1; nothing is promoted yet (2026-10-26).

Source: the r/ClaudeCode thread named in the title, read from a 17-page PDF export kept only on OSL-1046.
The post shows 887 votes and 187 comments.
The export shows no per-comment vote counts, so "prominence" below means position under Best sort, reply count, or the OP's own endorsement.
Paths below are repository-relative unless they start with `~/.claude`, which stands for `/home/AD.NORCERESEARCH.NO/hanf/.claude/plugins/cache/scribe/scribe/1.1.0/skills`.

## 1. Ideas most worth a bench, ranked

1. **Trust the code for what happens, and report every doc/code disagreement** (SirRobinBlibs, cites arXiv 2610.30571).
   Measure: seed a fixture hub with stale statements in `CLAUDE.md`, a `doc.go` and a `pattern/` file, run darn on tasks that touch them, and count the share of seeded conflicts the change description or a friction note reports, and the share where the agent copied the stale text.
2. **Never weaken, skip or delete a test or assertion to make a change pass** (NamerekDev, namrog84).
   Measure: per run, a diff scan of the task branch for removed `t.Run` cases, removed assertions, added `t.Skip` and deleted test functions, plus a planted task whose correct fix needs a test that is hard to satisfy.
3. **Read every file you need in one pass, then edit, then test once** (the post itself, 887 votes).
   Measure: on darn runs, token spend per run, `lym gate test` calls per run, Reads issued after the first Edit, and Code-Review findings of class `consistency` naming a missed sibling site.
4. **Before writing "we do X" or "we don't have X", reopen the code and cite `file:line`** (Stunning-Sherbet1853; OP said "stealing it").
   Measure: sample the factual claims about the codebase in change descriptions, decision records and board notes, check each against the code, and count false claims per run.
5. **Mutation check after writing tests** (namrog84: break one behavior on purpose and confirm a test fails).
   Measure: mutation score of the tests a run added or changed, computed over the changed packages by a Go mutation tool, compared across arms.
6. **A mistake names its instruction cause** (pixxelkick, adapted by Classic-Asparagus: "a missing, ambiguous, or conflicting instruction, or a clear instruction you did not follow").
   Measure: share of friction-filed issues that name a specific stencil or rule line as the cause, and the recurrence rate of the same issue in later runs after the cited line is fixed.
7. **Read the related tests before touching anything** (masiha97).
   Measure: first-gate failure rate per card or per darn commit, and self-fix attempts spent per card.
8. **Cheap model for the fresh-eyes reviewer** (pixxelkick: "spin up a sub agent with minimal context using a cheap model").
   Measure: run Code-Burler with the reviewer on a smaller model against the default, and compare findings per run, the fixer's dispute rate (false positives) and findings a later round or landing catches (false negatives), against token cost.

## 2. Every idea

### Read all, edit all, test once (post, 887 votes)

"Before changing anything, list every file you'll need and read them in one pass. Then make all edits, then run the tests once."
A reply (page 15) adds: keep one test run before the edits, so a failure at the end is attributable.

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: webster's FRESH-READ rule, `contracts/stencils/webster/webster-body-implementer.md:5-7`, and span reads via `lym quarry resolve` at `:53`; burler's pre-read for fork reviewers, `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-fork-reading.md:9-16`; twill's writer fork, `contracts/stencils/twill/twill-writer-fork.md:9`.
  The baseline half exists as webster's "a failure the card did not cause" test, `webster-body-implementer.md:113-122`, and drift's baseline, `contracts/stencils/drift/drift-template-baseline.md`.
- Missing: the darn writer gets no read-first rule and is told "Test as you work", `contracts/stencils/darn/darn-template-write.md:72-74`, the opposite of "test once".
- Where: `darn-template-write.md` Step 4.
- Bench: yes, see rank 3.

### Treat corrections as a queue, do not drop current work (pixxelkick, top comment)

- Verdict: does not fit as written; the orch analogue is already in place.
- Why: spawned agents take no mid-run operator corrections except recorded decisions (`lym loom decision add`, `.lym/orch/role.md:284`), and the orch puts every proposal "on the board as a note at once, never held in your head", `.lym/orch/role.md:324`.

### A mistake names its instruction cause; no apology (pixxelkick; Classic-Asparagus's `_observations/` folder and session reflection)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: friction notes, `contracts/stencils/friction/friction-directive-implementer.md:14-27`, filed by the reflection agent as issues, `contracts/stencils/friction/friction-template-reflection.md:122-163`; the no-apology tone rule, `~/.claude/conversation/SKILL.md:33`; orch workarounds go into the rules file with the issue number, `.lym/orch/role.md:353`.
- Missing: the friction directive asks what went wrong, not which instruction caused it (missing, ambiguous, conflicting, or clear but not followed), and the reflection agent does not classify by that.
- Where: the four `friction-directive-*.md` files and the reflection template.
- Bench: yes, see rank 6.

### YAGNI, no unasked scope, propose scope improvements separately (pixxelkick)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:27-34`; Code-Review flags unlicensed scope, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-rubric-code-review.md:62-63`, and so does plan review, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-rubric-plan-review.md:82`; follow-ups go on the board as notes, `darn-template-write.md:261`.

### Fresh-eyes reviewer sub-agent on a cheap model (pixxelkick)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: every review round is a fresh session, `contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml:71`, and model choice is per role, `contracts/specs/llm-model-spec.md`.
- Missing: evidence for which reviewer model is cost-effective.
- Bench: yes, see rank 8.

### "Make no mistakes", "it's for a children's hospital", "Codex said it could do better", "use a polite manner"

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: jokes or motivational framing with no mechanism to test.

### Never weaken or delete a test to make it pass; tests do not get edited to pass (NamerekDev, namrog84)

NamerekDev: "it stopped editing them. it deletes them now!"; a hook added for it was deleted by the next session.

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: only the webster verify-gate fixer, `contracts/stencils/webster/webster-body-verify-fix.md:26-27`; burler's fixer corrects a wrong assertion rather than adding tests, `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-step-fix.md:44`.
- Missing: the webster implementer, the darn writer, the burler fixer and the landing merge fixer (`contracts/stencils/landing/landing-template-fixer.md:31`, "fix the failing tests only") carry no such rule, and the Code-Review rubric does not flag a weakened test.
- Where: one shared rule rendered into every editing role, the way `contracts/stencils/edit/edit-directive.md` is, plus a Code-Review rubric line; a Go diff scan in the gate would make it structural, which matters given NamerekDev's hook story.
- Bench: yes, see rank 2.

### Mutation check after writing tests (namrog84)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: RED-before-GREEN, but only "when TDD is specified", `~/.claude/testing/SKILL.md:49-57`.
- Missing: no stencil or plan card asks for it.
- Where: the plan spec's test-card rules or the implementer stencil, or a `lym gate` step.
- Bench: yes, see rank 5.

### Review your work for creeping complexity and propose a workflow change (sammcj, partly cut off in the export); "keep it succinct" (es-ganso)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: review rounds judge design against the rubric; friction notes carry workflow proposals; brevity is `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:14-35`.

### Commit messages: short subject, body or not, no Co-Authored-By, task hash in the next commit (waruyamaZero, OP, howitzer1)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: subject shape `N: <name>`, `webster-body-implementer.md:68`; the landing writes the description and the trailer, `contracts/stencils/landing/landing-template-describe.md:49`.

### The agent you talk to never writes code; it supervises sub-agents (maniac56)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: "You diagnose; the run's own agents change the run", `.lym/orch/role.md:281`; webster's Master never reads code, `contracts/stencils/webster/webster-template-master.md:19`.

### Simplified Technical English; ban "load-bearing", em dashes, slop words (basskittens, bigtime_porgrammer, Icy-Excitement-467)

The OP replied that banning em dashes made the model use " - " instead: "swapped one tell for another".

- Verdict: partly, and not worth a bench.
- Have: `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:14-35`.
- Why not more: the operator's own skills use "load-bearing" (`~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:51`) and em dashes; a word ban trades one tell for another, as the OP saw.
  STE is the one variant with substance, since it constrains structure rather than banning tokens; it is a taste call for the operator, not a pipeline lever.

### Ask for a "go" before writing code; exploration mode; plan first, then `/grilling` (renatodinhani, holyknight00, getastatic)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: the pipeline is this: Discussion explores before asking, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-discussion.md:50-54`, then Plan, then Plan-Burler review rounds, which interrogate the plan before Webster writes code.

### "Do not guess"; prefer official docs; say when an answer rests only on training data (Whiteshovel66, TalShar)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: "Read the index below before guessing a `lym` command", `plugins/ly/skills/cli/SKILL.md:8`; Discussion reads code before asking, `loom-template-discussion.md:52-53`.
- Missing: nothing asks an agent to flag a claim about an external library or tool that it did not verify (go-git, cobra, tree-sitter, tmux, Claude Code flags).
- Where: `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md` or the implementer stencil.
- Bench: possible but weak: count first-gate compile failures on undefined symbols of external packages.

### Cite `file:line` before claiming "we do X" (Stunning-Sherbet1853)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: review findings need `path:line` evidence, `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-fix-check-rubric.md:18`, and disputes need cited text, `burler-step-fix.md:31`.
- Missing: change descriptions, decision records, board notes and orch replies make code claims with no citation rule; Discussion deliberately avoids `file:line` (`loom-template-discussion.md:57`), so the rule must target claims of presence or absence, not signatures.
- Where: `landing-template-describe*.md`, `darn-template-write.md` Step 5, the orch role's board section, and `~/.claude/conversation/SKILL.md` for chat.
- Bench: yes, see rank 4.

### "Clearly call out the next action" (4bitfocus)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: aimed at a solo chat loop where the human approves each step; runs are autonomous, and orch status reports already carry the attach command, `.lym/orch/role.md:393`.

### A repo map: one-line description per file, kept current (No_Dig_7017)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: `lym quarry toc`, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-plan.md:65`, fed by file headers and doc comments written to that bar, `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:113-120`.
- Missing: only the planner is pointed at it; the darn writer and burler reviewers are not.
- Where: `darn-template-write.md` Step 4 and `burler-step-1-explore.md`'s tool-use rules.
- Bench: possible: darn token spend and Reads before the first Edit, with and without the pointer; fold into the rank-3 bench rather than running it alone.

### No backward compatibility unless asked; update every call site (danielllenton)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:23-25`.

### Known-errors wiki per language, read before coding, appended after each own mistake (IxBetaXI)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: PATTERN plus `pattern/` and the orch rules play that role, with a size bound (`internal/pattern/headroom.go:7`); an agent-appended log would grow without review, which the headroom lint exists to stop.

### Skill-run logs and a weekly cron turning repeated actions into skills (bkrsh099)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: friction notes already carry the signal; the commenter says most generated skills get rejected.

### "Refactoring is harm": write `foo-2` beside `foo` (cjmurrr)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: conflicts with "no `_old`/`_v2` duplication — change the call sites", `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:24`; the thread itself rejects it.

### Do not rely on CLAUDE.md for secrets; block at the filesystem or proxy (radim11)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: guards live in code, `internal/shellguard` (package doc), and reed strips provider environment keys, `pattern/PATTERN-shuttle-provider-seam.md:9`.

### No system-wide `grep`/`find` (alanvnk: "nearly doubled the amount of sessions I can run")

- Verdict: worth adopting, if transcripts show it happens.
- Have: the plan spec scopes grep to a package, `contracts/specs/loom-plan-spec.md:370`.
- Where: a `internal/shellguard` row denying a recursive `grep`/`find`/`rg` rooted at `/` or `~`, since many parallel lym sessions share one machine.
- Bench: not needed; grep a sample of strand transcripts for such calls first.

### Replace CLAUDE.md lines with hooks and gates; a hook flags comments that will go stale (Neat-Culture9983 and parent)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: PATTERN entries enforced by tests, `CLAUDE.md:8`; `internal/shellguard`, `internal/commentlint`, `internal/patternlint`; the perishable-specific rule, `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md` "Don't pin a perishable specific".

### Docs and code disagree: follow the code, and report every inconsistency (SirRobinBlibs, arXiv 2610.30571: following the code went from 4.2% to 91.4% over 320 runs)

- Verdict: worth adopting, both halves (corrected by the operator, 2026-10-26).
- A description of behavior, in a `doc.go`, a `pattern/` file or `CLAUDE.md`, is not a rule: the code is the fact of what happens, so an agent that needs to know what the code does trusts the code, never a stale description.
  The code may still be wrong, so the mismatch is a finding, not a verdict: the agent silently fixes neither side and reports which side it believes is wrong.
  This is apart from `loom-rubric-code-review.md:66`, where a written rule on how new code should be written outranks a convention inferred from the surrounding code.
- Missing: no editing role is told to report a doc/code disagreement it meets, so a stale `doc.go` or `pattern/` line goes unreported.
- Where: one line in the implementer, darn writer and burler fixer stencils sending each disagreement to the change description or a friction note.
- Bench: yes, see rank 1.

### Call things what they are; do not invent terminology (actual-time-traveler, Classic-Asparagus)

- Verdict: does not fit for the project, partly for agents.
- Why: LoomYard coins its own names on purpose (weft, warp, reed, creel, dobby, batten); `CLAUDE.md:53` already confines the shorthands to conversation.
  An agent coining a new term in a stencil or doc comment is a review-level concern, not a bench.

### Ask one question before editing instead of guessing; say what you did not test (London-Boat)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: the question half is `~/.claude/conversation/SKILL.md:32` for chat and Discussion for runs (darn deliberately never blocks on a dialog, `darn-template-write.md:14`); the untested half is "anything to check or run by hand that was not run", `landing-template-describe.md:42` and `landing-template-describe-darn.md:39`.

### Hook at 50% context: wind down, hand off (puts_on_rddt)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: orch distill and refresh (`plugins/ly/skills/distill`, `plugins/ly/skills/refresh`), the orch handoff templates under `contracts/stencils/orch/`, and `scribe:handoff`; spawned strands are short-lived by design.

### "Do not suggest waiting until tomorrow"; human time estimates (extremelyhotdad)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: no agent schedules its own work; dobby drives runs.

### No new markdown file without asking; one fact, one owner file (SimplifAI_Life; pixxelkick on markdown litter)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:33-35`, `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:66-68`, `PATTERN-stencil-ownership` in `PATTERN.md`, scratch files under `.scratch/` (`contracts/stencils/edit/edit-directive.md:8`), and friction notes at a fixed path "with no filename of your own choosing".

### Every mistake becomes a rule or, better, a pre-work check (Weekly_Cat6537)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `CLAUDE.md:9` (a new invariant goes into PATTERN with its code), PATTERN entries marked `(test)`, and the orch workaround rule, `.lym/orch/role.md:353`.

### Keep CLAUDE.md under a page or it gets ignored (OP)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: no `CLAUDE.md` any more, and PATTERN growth is linted, `internal/pattern/headroom.go:7`.
- Missing: the orch role is 530 lines with hub rules inlined, and the stencils are long; nothing measures whether length costs compliance.
- Bench: possible and useful: a trimmed against a full orch role on replayed scenarios, counting violations of a fixed set of role rules.
  It is expensive to set up, so it ranks below the eight above.

### Read the related tests before touching code (masiha97)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: plan cards name the tests they change or reuse, `loom-template-plan.md:176-182`; burler's pre-read covers tests, `burler-fork-reading.md:14`.
- Missing: the darn writer and the merge fixer are not told to.
- Where: `darn-template-write.md` Step 4 and `landing-template-fixer.md`.
- Bench: yes, see rank 7.

### Explicit failure path: if X fails try Y, then report and stop (Joozio)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `PATTERN-refusal-way-forward` in `PATTERN.md`; the bounded self-fix and `NEEDS_PARENT`, `webster-body-implementer.md:108-130`.

### Block bulk edits with a hook so each file edit is visible (ghost_operative)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: LoomYard just allowed scripted edits on purpose (`contracts/stencils/edit/edit-directive.md`, commit `a1b6053a`); the scope guard and review read the diff instead.

### Some CLAUDE.md content belongs in a custom output style (thebigslapper)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: spawned agents get their instructions from stencils, not from CLAUDE.md or output styles.

## 3. Cheap enough to adopt without a bench

- One shared "never delete, skip or weaken a test or assertion to make it pass" rule for every editing role, copied from `webster-body-verify-fix.md:26-27`, plus a Code-Review rubric line flagging it.
  A bench is still worth running to see whether a prose rule suffices or a diff scan is needed.
- One line in the editing stencils: report each doc/code disagreement you meet in the change description or a friction note, trusting the code for what happens and naming the side it believes is wrong.
- Point the darn writer at `lym quarry toc` and at reading the tests of the code it changes, in `darn-template-write.md` Step 4.
- A friction-note prompt line asking for the instruction cause: missing, ambiguous, conflicting, or clear but not followed.
- A `shellguard` row against recursive searches rooted at `/` or the home directory, once a transcript sample shows they happen.

entries.title: A run keeps the lym binary and Bolt instructions it started with
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run reads its instructions live while it runs: the `lym` binary, and the stencils, specs and hub config on Bolt (`_board/_lym/{stencils,specs,config}`).
A landing deploys a new `lym` and can change those files, so a run started on one version can finish on another, such as a darn run that sat between its drift rows when `darn-drift-await-row` landed and its recipe changed under it (that landing wrote no transition code: such a run halts at Drift-Verify and is settled by hand with `lym drift waive`).
LoomYard takes no special care for such a run today, and the operator wants none written per change (operator, 2026-10-27).

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run keeps the version it started with, so nothing changes under it.
- Bolt: the run records the Bolt commit at its start and reads stencils, specs and config from that commit through git, in the one place those files are read, instead of from the working files; no copy is made.
- Binary: at the run's start the running `lym` is copied into a store under a name derived from its content, as the gate's prebuilt store does (`internal/gateslot`), and the run's driver and agents call that copy.
- Shared state stays live: the board, locks, gate slots, creel mail and the run's own records.
- One verb moves a run onto the newest version, for a run that needs a fix that landed after it started.

## Open

- Shared daemons (dobby, creel, gate) run the newest binary, so a pinned run's formats must stay readable by them, and a pinned binary must not write the board in an older format.
- Plugins and skills are loaded by Claude Code from one shared place and are left out of the first step.

entries.title: Windows lym opens land tiled on the right KDE virtual desktop
entries.brief: Konsole and VS Code windows opened by lym placed by desktop and tile on KDE Plasma
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-28)

The operator runs KDE Plasma with virtual desktops and tiling.
The Konsole windows lym opens on a run's worktree (`lym reed window`, batten's terminal for each run) and the VS Code windows it opens (`lym ide`) land wherever KWin puts them, untiled and on the current desktop, so the operator moves and tiles each by hand.

## Idea

A window lym opens lands tiled on the right virtual desktop by itself.
How the placement rules are written and kept is open (operator, 2026-10-28); the candidates:

- KWin window rules (`kwinrulesrc`) that match the window title or class lym already sets, such as the reed window's `--title` and the VS Code window title `lym ide seed` writes (a hub or beam workspace file now sets `window.title` to `<SHORTNAME>: <name> workspace`, since `ide-seed-workspace-and-keys`), and assign desktop and position.
  KWin keeps them, and lym only names its windows predictably; lym could write or check the rules from a config of its own.
- lym places each window after opening it, through KWin's D-Bus or a KWin script, from a config that maps a window kind (orch, run, IDE) to a desktop and a tile.
- Plasma 6 tiling: whether a rule or a script can put a window into a named custom tile, or only on a desktop and screen edge, is to be found out first.

Whatever the route, lym hard-codes no desktop environment: the placement is a config choice that does nothing on a machine without KDE.

## Open

- Which windows: run terminals only, or the orch's and VS Code too.
- The mapping: one desktop per run, per hub, or per window kind.
- Whether lym writes the rules or the operator does, with lym only keeping its window titles stable.

entries.title: A landing notice on request, per task
entries.brief: A landing notice from dobby on request, per task, reusing the wait that lym hibernate request --after has
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-28)

A run that lands sends nothing: the orch learns of a landing only when something else wakes it, and the orch never polls runs.
When the operator asks the orch to report a run's result as soon as it lands, the orch cannot keep that promise, and the operator has to ask again.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-28 and 2026-10-30)

Dobby sends the notice, never batten: dobby drives each run to its end, knows its outcome and landing commit, and already mails the orch.
No process of its own is needed, since dobby only keeps a list of watches and reads the run state it already has.

- The orch sets a watch when the operator asks, through a verb of its own, for one slug; it is never on by default for every run, and it can be withdrawn.
- When the watched run lands, or ends without landing, dobby posts one short creel line to the orch naming the slug, the outcome and the landing commit.
- The watch ends when it has fired once.
- The test for a run past its Land row is the one `lym hibernate request --after` already has (`landFinished` in `internal/hibernateengine`); it is taken out into one shared piece that hibernate and dobby both use, never copied.
- The hibernate daemon stays as it is: only its wait is shared.

## Open

- Where dobby keeps the watch: a flag on the board entry or a record of its own.
- The shared test says only that a run is past Land, so it must also tell a run that landed from one that ended without landing, since the notice names the outcome.
- The verb's name and where it lives.
- Whether the hibernate request should move into dobby as well: it spans every beam, since `--after-all` waits on all runs while a dobby sees its own, and a hub pause must leave the dobby that waits outside it.

entries.title: Dobby sends the run notices, not a row of the batten recipe
entries.brief: Move quiet, driver-dead and api-error detection from battenshed/notice.go into dobby loop over the runs it drives
entries.body:
## Seen

The quiet, driver-dead, api-error and usage-limit notices are built in `internal/battenshed/notice.go`, as a row of each batten run's own recipe, and run inside the pass dobby spawns for that run (operator, 2026-10-29).
They go out as `[batten notice]` lines from `ly:BATTEN`, and the orch role, the stencils and the hub's rules read that line.
Dobby is the daemon that keeps track of the runs and the common driver of every one under its beam, the pawl run of a beam included, which the dobby of the beam's parent drives.
Batten is only a profile of a shed, and a shed drives nothing itself: it is driven by dobby.
Dobby's loop already reads every run's state, writes a heartbeat and posts its own notices, so it sees what each notice needs.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-29 and 2026-10-30)

Dobby detects and sends these notices itself, in its loop over the runs it drives, and the batten recipe keeps no notice row.
A run waiting on a person, such as a pull request, is read by the same loop through the wait markers it already honours, so a long wait never reads as a stall.
The detection logic, its keys and its idle clocks move as they are; only the place that runs them changes.

- The marker file that records the notices already sent, one episode key per line, moves to dobby, and lives under `_lym`, so it survives a dobby re-exec and a machine switch.
  It is the existing marker moved, never a new notification flag; the set of notices dobby looks for stays fixed in the code.
- The notice lines are sent by dobby, from `<shortname>:DOBBY`, and read `[dobby notice]` in place of `[batten notice]`.
  The orch role's Notices section, the stencils and the hub's rules that name the old line change in the same task.
- The notices of a run stay with the dobby of the machine that drives it; the orch is not the same on another machine either.

entries.title: Stop-hook creel mail arrives twice and is labelled as an error
entries.brief: One creel mail shows twice at the Stop hook, once as feedback and once as Stop hook error, with the hook command text in the model context
entries.body:
## Fixed (2026-10-30)

The `creel-mail-delivered-once` landing fixed this: a Stop delivery now prints `additionalContext` alone with no error label, the idle ring hands the mail over once, and the model and the operator each see a mail once.
The note stays until the operator confirms with the tier3 `TestSmokeCreelHookDelivery` smoke on a real session.

## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-29)

Each creel mail reaches the operator's terminal twice at a Stop hook:

- a `Stop hook feedback` block headed `Stop says: [creel] #N from ...` with the mail text;
- then `Ran 2 stop hooks` with a `Stop hook error: [creel] Mail for you arrived... additional context` line and a second `Stop hook feedback: [creel] #N ...` with the mail text again.

A normal delivery is labelled `Stop hook error`, and the hook command text reaches the model.
The installed `lym` carries the fix of `creel-hook-delivery-fixes`, so the bug stands in the current build.

## Expected

One message per mail, delivered once, labelled as a delivery and not as an error, with no hook command text in the model's context.

entries.title: Dobby never starts a task whose slug has an old finished run record, and status gives no reason
entries.brief: A ready task sat unstarted for over an hour: batten refused its slug every pass, and beam status read ready to start
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-29)

The released task `claude-md-lym-rules-out` did not start for over an hour.
`lym beam status` showed it as `ready to start`, with room under the run limit and no dependency, and gave no reason.
`.lym/beam/dobby.log` showed dobby trying to start it about every 30 seconds from 13:43:17Z, each pass failing with `battencli: "claude-md-lym-rules-out" has already completed; to run it again, run "lym batten cleanup --apply" from the prime ...`.
The cause was an old run record for the same slug, `_lym/shed/claude-md-lym-rules-out/`, from machine `neve`, 2026-10-28, ended at Worktree-Teardown.
This hub's prime is on `osl-1046`, and the operator knows of no run of that slug on Neve; why the record read as done is not known.
`lym batten cleanup --apply` removed the record, after which no branch of that name was left locally or on the remote.

## Idea

- `lym beam status` states why a ready task is not started, with the refusal dobby last got, so `ready to start` is never shown with no reason.
- The start of a task whose slug has an old finished run record is handled where the task is released or where dobby starts it, with a message that names the way forward, instead of failing every pass.
- Find out where a run record of another machine came from for a slug this hub had not run.

entries.title: Dobby's notice for a start that keeps failing reached the orch over an hour late
entries.brief: Dobby failed to start a task every pass from 13:43Z, but its mail reached the orch only an hour later
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-29)

Dobby failed to start the released task `claude-md-lym-rules-out` on every pass from 13:43:17Z, about every 30 seconds, and the orch heard nothing.
Its mail, creel #34 from `ly:DOBBY` with the text `dobby could not start the task`, reached the orch only after more than an hour, right after the orch ran `lym batten cleanup --apply`.
The orch found the cause by asking `lym beam status` and reading `.lym/beam/dobby.log` through a fork, after the operator noticed the task had not started.
The role says dobby sends a line for a refused start and for a pass that keeps failing, so the notice should have come within a few passes.

## Idea

- Find out why the notice came late: whether dobby sends it only after many failed passes, whether the send was held, or whether creel delivered it late.
- A refused start or a pass that keeps failing reaches the orch within a few passes, and a start that keeps failing with the same error does not resend it every pass.

entries.title: Prove the dotnet scoper, shared build and Drift on the C# sandbox hub
entries.brief: Switch the sandbox gate to scoper dotnet, a build step and --no-build, then enable Drift there
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-29)

The sandbox hub `lym-csharp-LYMHUB` (shortname `cs`, anchor `lym-csharp/dotnet`, over `Knatte18/lym-csharp`) ran its first darn run, `friction-colebrook`, end to end, and it landed as `7f50ffe`.
Its gate is the simple form: `tier0` runs `dotnet test` without `Category=Slow` and `tier1` with it, with no `scoper`, no `build` step and no `--no-build`.
So the dotnet scoper, the shared build and Drift are not proved on a C# repository.
The first `tier1` gate run on Neve died with "Internal CLR error (0x80131506)" after 900 s and passed on a rerun; the cause is unknown.

## Idea

Switch the sandbox gate to `scoper: dotnet`, a `build` step and `--no-build`, so the scoper and the shared build are proved there, then turn on `drift.enabled` there to prove Drift, before any C# hub that holds proprietary code relies on them.
The hub's setup is in `docs/dotnet-hub.md`; the sandbox stays the place to reproduce a lym fault another C# hub shows.

entries.title: Creel mail between hubs through an inbox folder, with a verified sender
entries.brief: A shared inbox folder takes mail from other hubs; each file names the sender hub and agent so a reply knows where to go
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

The operator sometimes has the orch write straight into another repository, such as Scribe or Quarry, and would rather let the orchs of the hubs talk to each other, which is how lym is meant to be used.
Creel has no support for this today.
One daemon serves one hub, its socket is named from the hub path, and the hub a call reaches is the hub of the directory it runs from.
A process outside the hub's strands is `EXTERNAL`, shown with a terminal and parent-process envelope, and its replies reach only a waiting `post --wait-reply`.
`EXTERNAL` is the wrong sender for this: the receiver must see the real strand that sent the message.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-30)

A shared inbox folder takes in messages from outside the hub.
The file a message becomes carries its sender: the path of the sender hub's inbox folder and the name of the agent that sent it.
A message needs a receiver, so the daemon knows whom to give it to.
A reply is addressed from those two fields, so the replier knows which agent in which hub to answer.

## Verifying the sender (operator, 2026-10-30)

A file cannot prove its sender: any process of the same user can write one, so a prompt-injected agent could write `ly:orch` in the sender field.
The sending daemon, which reads the caller from `SO_PEERCRED` as it does today, writes the file.
The receiving daemon then asks the sending hub's daemon to confirm it:

1. The file names the sender hub's path, and the receiver derives that hub's socket name from it, as `creel-<shortname>-<hash>.sock`, with no registry.
2. The receiver sends one call in creel's JSON-lines protocol, such as `confirm`, with the message id, the receiver and a hash of the text.
3. The sender's daemon looks in its own journal for a message from that strand to that receiver with that hash, and answers yes or no, never the text.
4. Only on yes does the receiver show the sender as that strand; otherwise the message shows as unverified.

This is a call and not a signature on the file, since a signature needs a secret and every agent of the same user can read a secret file; the sending daemon cannot be fooled, because it reads its caller from the process and knows what it sent.
A message can be confirmed once, so a copied file cannot be reused.
The journal's retention bounds how late a confirmation can come, so the receiver confirms when the message arrives.
A sending daemon that is down is started as a client starts it today, or the message stays unverified.
The check works only within one user, since the sockets do.

## Open design points

- Where the folder lives and how a sender addresses a hub: a path derived from the hub path, like the socket, and a record on the machine that maps a shortname to a hub path.
- What a reply does across the hub border: it goes to the sender's inbox folder, addressed to the agent the file names.
- How a role treats mail from another hub: as data to weigh, never as the operator's instruction, since it is a channel for prompt injection into the receiving orch.
- How this fits a closed area for lym's process tree (research note `sandboxing-options-2026-10-30`): the folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.
- Another machine: a folder that a synced directory carries would reach a hub on Neve; not designed here.

entries.title: A closed area for lym: bwrap sandbox in stages, off by default
entries.brief: Run the lym process tree in a bwrap area with a host proxy and broker, built in three stages with a stop; to be split if it goes ahead
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

Every agent lym starts runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which many people do not accept, and a repository that states it supports safe sandboxing is worth more than one that does not.
The operator uses lym alone, on Linux (OSL-1046: Ubuntu 24.04; Neve: Kubuntu on Ubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6), and has no interest in other users or in Windows.
The research is `docs/research/sandboxing-options-2026-10-30.md`: it weighs `bwrap`, Landlock, a dedicated Linux user, systemd sandboxing, podman and Claude Code's own `/sandbox`, and the packages and cards each would change.

Two exposures hold today with no area: an agent can reach `/run/user/<uid>/bus` and through it `systemd-run --user`, which starts any process outside lym's tree, and it can type into other hubs' tmux panes through their sockets in `/tmp/tmux-<uid>`, the Models hub's among them.

## Idea

Run the whole lym process tree inside a `bwrap` area launched by lym itself, with the agents free inside it and a short, controlled list of exits.
It is an option the operator turns on, never a requirement: with it off, everything works as it does today, and with it on, nothing starts when the sandbox cannot.
The operator thinks the full design is complicated and error-prone, and doubts it will work without large problems, so it is built in stages with a stop between them.
This is one large note and is split into tasks, or a project, only when the operator decides it goes ahead.

### Before the area: two cheap steps

- Start a hub's tmux server from a Konsole window, not a VS Code terminal: the server inherits the `vscode` AppArmor profile, which grants user namespaces to every agent of the hub.
- A line in `README.md` that every agent lym starts runs with bypass permissions, and that lym belongs on a machine the operator is willing to hand to its agents.

### Stage 1: the filesystem area only

`bwrap` with `--unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv` around reed's tmux server and everything under it, started by a new `lym area start` and a supervisor inside.

- The hub is bound read-write at its own path, since the tmux server name, the creel socket name, git's worktree links and Claude Code's transcript directory all derive from absolute paths; `/usr`, `/etc` and `/opt` are read-only, `$HOME` a tmpfs with read-only binds of the Go toolchain, the Claude Code binary and the installed `lym`.
- The area has its own Claude config directory and Go caches bound at the usual paths, with the host's plugin cache read-only on top, so the host's `settings.json` hooks never run in it.
- One host directory holds the tmux socket directory, so `lym reed attach` from outside drives the server inside; tried on OSL-1046 with a tmux server inside `bwrap`.
- `.git/hooks` is read-only; `.git/config` stays writable, since `internal/gitrepo/branchmark.go` writes `branch.<b>.lymLocal` into it.
- Network stays open and there is no broker, so the landing deploy, `lym reed window`, `lym ide` and `lym hibernate request` do not work from inside; the operator does them by hand, from outside.
- A config module `area` with `required`, off by default; `lym area start` refuses on any failure and never falls back to an unsandboxed start.
- Ubuntu 24.04 needs a one-time AppArmor profile for `/usr/bin/bwrap`, loaded by root; the report names the profile, and Ubuntu 25.04 and later ship it, which is not verified on Neve.

This closes the two exposures above and shows early whether tmux, creel and dobby run well inside an area.

### Stop: the operator decides whether stage 1 works well enough to go on.

### Stage 2: egress through a host proxy

No network inside the area; a host-side proxy, reached through a bound socket, allows CONNECT to `api.anthropic.com`, `claude.ai`, `platform.claude.com`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `github.com` and `api.github.com`, with a loopback relay inside the area.
Telemetry and the auto-updater are off by environment.
The GitHub token handed to the area is fine-grained and limited to the hub's repositories; the operator's `gh` login never enters.
WebFetch and the `prowler` skill reach only these hosts.

### Stage 3: a broker for the remaining exits

A host-side process serving a fixed set of verbs and never a command line from the area: the landing deploy (it fetches `origin/main` into its own clone, checks the commit is the tip, builds with the host's Go and installs), `lym reed window` opening Konsole, and `lym hibernate request`.
`lym ide` is refused, since VS Code on the host would run git over repositories the area writes; the host runs no git over the area's repositories at all.

## What is not claimed

Isolation from a kernel exploit, which needs a virtual machine; that data in the area cannot leave through an allowed host; and that a landed change of lym itself cannot run on the host once deployed, which matters on this hub because it develops lym.
Landlock stays a possible inner layer once both machines run a kernel with ABI 9 and 10, and Claude Code deny rules in shuttle's settings are a cheap second line inside the area; the dedicated user, podman, systemd sandboxing and Claude Code's `/sandbox` inside lym runs are left out.
The report estimates the whole at five tasks and eighteen cards.

## Related

Note `creel-cross-hub-mail`: the inbox folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.

entries.title: pr-continue wakes the PR-Review wait at once
entries.brief: The PR-Review wait sleeps up to a minute between wakes, so lym loom pr-continue takes effect up to a minute late
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-30)

On the first PR-Review run, the reviewer agent ran `lym loom pr-continue` and the run went on only after a while.
The wait sleeps between wakes, from a floor of one second up to a ceiling of one minute while nothing changes (`prWaitFloor`, `prWaitCeiling` in `internal/landingshed/prreview.go`), and `pr-continue` only sets a flag that the next wake reads.
Finalize's gate then runs on the landed tree as for any landing, which takes minutes by itself.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-30)

`lym loom pr-continue` wakes the waiting row at once, so the PR is closed and Finalize begins with no wait of up to a minute.

entries.title: Gate runs spend much of their time starting processes: start fewer
entries.brief: launch_seconds is a large share of a gate run on OSL-1046, where each process start is slow; the aim is a faster gate by starting fewer processes
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-30)

Runs are slow on OSL-1046, gates above all, and every process start there is expensive.
`lym gate report --slug pr-review-empty-branch` shows `launch_seconds` of 266 of 639 s wall for `code-burler-fix` and 153 of 516 s for `darn-write`, with a wait for a gate slot of about zero: the time is in the test runs, and a large part of it in starting processes.

## Idea

The aim is a faster gate run, by starting fewer processes per run.
- Find what a gate run launches: how many test binaries, `go` invocations and helper processes per tier, and which of them repeat from one gate key to the next.
- Cut the launches: link several packages' tests into fewer binaries, or reuse a built test binary across the gate keys of one run, wherever the result stays the same.
- Measure a gate run before and after, so the gain is known; the measurement runs as a darn task with profile `docs`.

entries.title: README shows each project's slug
entries.brief: A project section in the README, and its page, show the project slug beside handle and title.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

The README's section for a project shows its handle and title but not its slug, so the reader cannot tell which slug to name in a command.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-30)

- Each project section in the README shows the project's slug beside its handle and title, for instance in the section heading.
- A project page shows the slug too, if it does not already.
- Nothing else in the rendering changes.
